title: The harvest's tenth
hook: a tenth of rain-watered crops, a twentieth of irrigated ones

segments.voice: Yesterday, gold, trade, crops and herds, and your line: each wealth has its share. Did you sort what you live with from what just sits? Today, the end of a week, and the crops. Day one thousand ninety-nine.

Two fields, side by side, the same wheat in each. On the first, the farmer did almost nothing for the water. Clouds came over, rain fell, the ground drank, and the wheat came up. On the second, the farmer had to work for every drop: a well, a bucket, an animal turning a wheel, hour after hour, carrying water up out of the ground. Harvest day comes for both. Same crop. Same weight in the barn. Does the second farmer owe the same as the first? The answer in the hadith is no, and the reason is in the sky. Today, the harvest's tenth.
screen: `TWO FIELDS, THE SAME WHEAT.` → `ONE RAIN-FED, ONE HAND-WATERED.` → `DO THEY OWE THE SAME?`

segments.voice: First, the rule. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari, from Ibn Umar, says that on what is watered by the rain or by springs, or draws its own water, the share is a tenth. On what is watered by drawing water, the share is half a tenth. A tenth, or a twentieth. The Arabic word for that tenth is 'ushr. Second, the reason, as scholars explain it. The first farmer's water came free, from the sky. The second farmer paid for his, in labor and cost. So the share follows the gift: where more was simply given, more is given back. That's why your line is rain's share. The extra in the first field's due is, in a sense, the rain's part. Third, the timing. You met it on the day of the hawl: the Qur'an tells farmers to give the due on the day of the harvest. No year to wait. And a threshold applies here too, given in loads of grain in the same report you met with the nisab. Fourth, set this week's pieces side by side. Zakat, the word that means to purify and to grow. Who pays: from their rich, to their poor. The threshold, below which a person is protected. One in forty for savings. The year of moons. Four kinds of wealth. And today, the field: a tenth or a twentieth, depending on the rain. Read together, the rules can be heard asking one question in different ways: what was received, and how much of it came without anyone's doing? Tomorrow, the other side of the ledger: who receives it.
screen: `A TENTH, OR HALF A TENTH.` · `THE SHARE FOLLOWS THE GIFT.` · `GIVEN ON THE HARVEST DAY.` · `THIS WEEK, ONE PICTURE.` · then, large: `RAIN'S SHARE.`

segments.voice: The practice: give thanks for rain. In Sahih al-Bukhari, when the Prophet ﷺ saw rain, he would ask for it to be a beneficial rain: allahumma sayyiban nafi'an. If you pray, you can say those words now, or simply alhamdulillah. If you don't, sit and remember the last rain you heard. The sound on a window. The smell of the street afterward. Then follow it: into soil, into wheat, into the bread you ate this week. Breathe with that chain. The bell holds the time.
The harvest's tenth. 'Ushr: a tenth of rain-watered crops, a twentieth of crops watered by labor, given on the harvest day. Today's word.
Your line: rain's share. Today, when you eat bread or rice or fruit, think of the rain behind it, and the share it asks for. Tomorrow: the eight, in depth. Day one thousand ninety-nine.

howItsDone: Muslim farmers whose harvest passes the threshold give a tenth of rain-fed crops and a twentieth of irrigated crops at harvest time, following the hadith of Ibn Umar.

myth: every crop owes the same share, however it was watered
rain or springs: a tenth. water drawn by labor: half a tenth.
a threshold applies to the harvest too
the same report you met with the nisab gives it in loads of grain.
the hadith on the tenth and the twentieth is in Sahih al-Bukhari

fork.setup: you're the second farmer. you hauled every drop from a well all season. harvest day: what share does the hadith ask of you?
options: a tenth, the same as the rain-fed field.
nothing, because you worked for it.
fork.reveal: half a tenth. your labor is counted, so the share is smaller. the rain-fed field gives more, because more was given to it.

original.note: Arabic: the tenth, the share of a rain-watered harvest.

trapdoor: what you thought: a crop tax is a crop tax.
what it means: a tenth when the water came free, a twentieth when it was drawn by labor, given on the harvest day.
what a scholar hears: Ibn Umar's report in Bukhari ties the share to the cost of water, so the rule weighs what was given against what was worked for.

notes: Bukhari 1483 (Ibn Umar: a tenth on rain, springs or 'athari'; half a tenth on what is watered by drawing): confirm number and the paraphrase 'draws its own water' for 'athari'.
Bukhari 1032 ('allahumma sayyiban nafi'an' on seeing rain): confirm number and transliteration. It is quoted as the Prophet's own words, not a new prayer.
'The share follows the gift' and 'rain's part' are offered as the scholars' explanation of the cost-of-water reasoning; confirm framing.
